name: George Burchett cosmetic tattooing

card.summary: Early-20th-century cosmetic tattooing by British tattooist George Burchett, who by the 1930s was tattooing permanent colour onto eyebrows and complexions to give a defined, made-up look without daily makeup.
card.note: Modern reviews describe pigment migration, granulomas, scarring and infection risks for cosmetic tattoos.

quick.overview:
George Burchett (1872-1953) was a London tattooist billed as the King of Tattooists. In the 1930s he is credited with developing cosmetic tattooing, including permanently darkening eyebrows, an early form of what is now called permanent makeup.

The appeal was a defined brow, colour or complexion that stays put without daily application. His own memoirs (published posthumously) say salons tattooed many women as a complexion treatment, and the technique grew into the eyebrow, eyeliner and lip tattooing offered today.
quick.how: In practice the work meant implanting pigment into the skin with needles to mimic brow hair or add colour. Modern descendants include machine-driven shading and microblading, where tiny hand-cut strokes imitate hairs; results fade over months and are topped up with touch-ups.
quick.risks: Dermatology reviews list infection, allergic reactions, granulomas, scarring, blurred or migrating pigment and fading or colour change as complications of cosmetic tattooing; rare reports link cosmetic tattoos to sarcoid reactions and to burning sensations during MRI. Removal can be difficult.

lead: George Burchett (born George Burchett-Davis, 1872-1953) was an English tattooist known as the King of Tattooists, who worked from studios in London and counted royalty among his clients.[1] He is credited with developing cosmetic tattooing in the 1930s; the one specific example given in his biography is the permanent darkening of eyebrows.[1]

For people interested in appearance, the idea behind his work was that pigment placed in the skin could give brows, lips or cheeks a defined, made-up look that does not need to be redrawn each morning. Wikipedia's article on permanent makeup notes that Burchett's memoirs say beauty salons tattooed many women as a 'complexion treatment', and that an earlier London tattooist, Sutherland MacDonald, was documented tattooing colour onto pale cheeks in 1902.[2]

Cosmetic tattooing grew considerably from the 1970s and 1980s, and dermatology reviews now describe eyebrow microblading, eyeliner and lip tattooing as widely popular, alongside documented complications.[3][4]

chain: Pigment is tattooed into the skin
Brows, lips or cheeks keep a defined colour
angle.text: Burchett's cosmetic tattooing put permanent colour into the skin, most clearly on the eyebrows, so the face looked groomed and defined without daily application. Its modern forms (microblading, lip and eyeliner tattooing) are used the same way.

paras: Burchett was born in Brighton in 1872, was expelled from school at 12 for tattooing classmates and joined the Royal Navy at 13, where he developed his skills.[1] He became a full-time tattooist in 1900 with studios on Mile End Road and Waterloo Road in London and attracted wealthy and royal clients, among them Alfonso XIII of Spain and Frederik IX of Denmark.[1]

In the 1930s he developed cosmetic tattooing, with eyebrow darkening given as the specific example.[1] Wikipedia's permanent makeup article describes him as a major developer of the technique in that decade and says his memoirs recount salons tattooing many women under the label of a complexion treatment.[2] That article also credits Sutherland MacDonald with earlier, well-documented work colouring pale cheeks in 1902.[2]

Memoirs of a Tattooist appeared in 1958, five years after his death, credited to 'Peter Leighton' (a pseudonym of Edward Spiro). Later research has found its text drew largely on newspaper articles written after his death rather than on his own notes.[1]

Permanent makeup became more common in the 1970s and 1980s, initially for hair and pigment loss from disease, and now covers eyebrows, eyeliner, lip colour, areola recolouring and scar camouflage.[2] A 2022 review describes cosmetic tattooing as having advanced over the past 50 years alongside social media and internet access.[3] Microblading, which tattoos hair-like strokes by hand with a small blade, is now a leading eyebrow technique; the strokes fade over months and need touch-ups.[4]

No studies of Burchett's own work exist. Modern reviews of cosmetic tattooing describe early complications (infections including herpes simplex, healing problems, dissatisfaction with results) and late ones (fading, colour shift, pigment 'blowout' into surrounding skin, nodules and granulomas, allergic reactions in lip tattoos, scarring after microblading).[5] Case reports describe sarcoid granulomas, including systemic sarcoidosis, triggered by cosmetic tattoos, with iron oxide pigments hypothesised as a factor.[6] A 1996 Lancet report described hepatitis C transmission linked to cosmetic tattooing in women.[7]

Reviews and the Wikipedia article note possible allergic reactions, infection, keloids, scarring, pigment migration and, rarely, swelling or burning during MRI.[2][5] Removal can be difficult and may require laser treatment.[2][4]

timeline.event: Becomes a full-time tattooist in London.[1]
